claims.text: The baseline W–Cu composite consists of tungsten particles embedded in a continuous copper matrix.
CVD can deposit a thin, uniform WC coating on tungsten particles before copper infiltration.
The proposed CVD treatment is performed at 900–1200 °C in a controlled carbon-rich atmosphere.
The intervention produces a nanometric WC interlayer between tungsten and copper.
The resulting WC interlayer is coherent.
The WC interlayer provides a graded acoustic-impedance transition between tungsten and copper.
The WC interlayer provides a graded electron-band-structure transition between tungsten and copper.
The graded interfacial transition reduces thermal resistance at the tungsten–copper interface.
Reduced tungsten–copper interfacial thermal resistance increases the composite's effective thermal conductivity.
WC has sufficient inherent hardness to support mechanical load transfer across the interface.
The chemical stability of WC helps maintain irradiation tolerance.
The WC-interlayered composite will have a statistically significant increase in effective thermal conductivity relative to an otherwise comparable unmodified W–Cu composite.
The WC-interlayered composite will retain mechanical durability relative to the unmodified W–Cu control.
The WC-interlayered composite will retain irradiation resistance relative to the unmodified W–Cu control.
Optimizing WC interlayer thickness can prevent the interlayer from introducing unacceptable brittleness.
The predicted benefits should persist during thermal cycling up to approximately 500 °C.
The predicted benefits should persist at irradiation doses typical of fusion-reactor joint environments.
